utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. So do we have the appearances now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry and Mr. Huber for the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours my name is Zejnil Olujic, attorney from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague Tomislav Kuzmonovic, attorney from the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and I represent Esad Landzo, along with my colleague, Ms. Nancy Boler. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We're having some difficulties with the transcripts. Mr. Olujic, I think you start this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, thank you. Before we begin with the witnesses for the Defence, allow me in an introductory address to present our Defence and the purpose for the testimony of our witnesses, which we will bring before this Honourable Court. My wish is first to illustrate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You know this was a choice given to Defence, if the intent to make an opening address during their Defence, they should not make an opening speech. Mr. Topolskovic made a long opening speech and lost his right to make a Defence speech. If you read the rules carefully, you see the implications of making them. But I suppose we might allow you, you were not part of the team then. Although, you should have known what your predecessor has done before now. But, in any event, I think you could do that, you can explain whatever you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. What I should like to start with is to make a preliminary analysis of the indictment and the overall proceedings against my client, Mr. Zdravko Mucic. I shall then present a further review--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You're merely going to explain what your evidence, Defence evidence, will be. It's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: A general opening speech introducing everything, analysis, defence, indictment, those are not the things you're expected to do at this stage. If you choose to do that, then you could have done that at the opening or at the end of your evidence because you always have a right to address the Trial Chamber at the end of the Defence evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your advice, Your Honours, I am aware of that. I do not intend to summarise all the things that I consider important to be said in my closing statement. I should just like to familiarise you in brief with the proceedings so far and the method in which we intend to present our witnesses and prove the link between the Defence witnesses of Mr. Mucic and the proceedings so far and the indictment. This would then lead to my conclusions. This will certainly not be a closing speech, that will come in due course. But, since there has been a change, if I can call it that, in the strategy of Defence, when I joined the Defence team in May, 1997, the Trial Chamber allowed me the possibility to make this introductory address, especially in view of my learned colleague who represented the Defence before me. So first of all, I should like to analyse the indictment against Mr. Mucic, then I should like to comment on the actual arrest procedure in the Town of Vienna, Austria. We know that Mr. Mucic was arrested by the Austrian police in an anti-terrorist operation, even though he was charged with so-called objective responsibility. A man who knew that he had not consciously done anything wrong, he was naturally afraid and depressed by such an operation. He was not immediately given access to a sworn court interpreter, which in the opinion of Mr. Mucic was a further illegal act against him. What is important now is not that the responsibility for this lies with the Austrian police, but rather the fact that Mucic was depressed and that there was a demonstration of force at his expense. The very absence of an official interpreter resulted in certain consequences. His daughter interpreted for him, who is legally unqualified and has a poor knowledge of the German language. And there's no doubt that in the process of interpretation, she made a series of errors. There was no one there to check her work because no one on site was familiar with both languages, that is German and Croatian. Further, my client received a series of incorrect data from the Austrian authorities. The Austrian law regulates remand prison in quite a different manner from the statute and rules of procedure of this learned tribunal. After his daughter interpreted to him the information given by the Austrian police, correctly or incorrectly, then the Austrian judge spoke to him and gave him a form with provisions interpreted by the official, sworn interpreter and quite contrary to the rules of this lofty Tribunal. A third series of incorrect acts were carried out by the investigator. The investigator clearly disinformed Mr. Mucic, for he gave him information contained in the statute having to do with the rights of detainees, but he did not convey them to him in the manner envisioned by the statute. So that the question one may ask is, why he didn't do that? Why the text of the statute and the rules were not read out to him literally, but rather, interpreted in a way which is certainly affected by the consciousness and the experience of the investigator and the background he comes from? It was quite simple to find the articles and rules, to cite them literally from the text. As a result, Mr. Mucic was disinformed and this was at his expense. What the daughter of Mr. Mucic interpreted to him as written in the Austrian forms is quite contrary to the provisions of this Tribunal. Even what the investigator himself told him was not identical, so that Mr. Mucic is in a detrimental position. Under these circumstances, after a long day of not having had anything to eat, Mr. Mucic was kept awake until 2.00 a.m. and questioned. He was totally disinformed about the very cause of his arrest. The investigators told him a falsehood that he was arrested for murder and rape without showing him the grounds on which the charges of objective responsibility rested. Naturally, such a tormented and frightened man, knowing well that he had not committed any crime, gave up his rights and all he wanted to do was to go home feeling that this was just a mistake. He doesn't realise why he should apply any kind of tactics, why he should call an attorney and he doesn't even know that he's entitled to one. He simply wants everything to be cleared up. He wants to go home and that is why he renounced his rights as envisioned by the statute. The Austrian judge, the Austrian attorney and the Austrian police around him and who are not familiar with the statutes of this Court, still interfered. The attorney promised to get him out of prison after two weeks if he engages him, even though he himself knows nothing about the case. The restrictive Austrian law prohibits Mr. Mucic from speaking in any language other than German when making the single telephone call that he is entitled to and this is written in the Austrian law. Our question is, how could Mr. Mucic could have engaged anyone like that? Why, even before the arrest, didn't the Croatian embassy in Vienna interfere? If it had, it could have provided Mr. Mucic both with an interpreter and a Defence attorney. As my distinguished colleague Tapuskovic from Serbia, a country which is, allegedly, belongs to the accused in these proceedings and which, according to you, committed a military aggression against the party to which Mr. Mucic belonged, this is quite unclear the us. And all this is part of the injustice in the proceedings done to Mr. Mucic. In this way, he was deprived of many rights. That is why the knowledge and the documents obtained in Vienna in this way could not be appropriate for the Court to make any rulings on their basis. An analysis of the indictment itself. The indictment charges Mr. Mucic of being in a position of superior responsibility and holds him responsible for this. However, the statute of this Tribunal does not use this term at all. Therefore, the indictment charges the accused with something that is not -- that does not figure in the statute. What does a position of superiority mean? That is unclear. A teacher in school is a superior, a traffic policeman in traffic, a doctor in a surgery. Therefore, until this superiority is explained, the indictment is lacking. Second, the indictment says that Mr. Mucic was a superior to those who came to the Celebici camp. Here again we are not told what particular kind of superiority in question. Third, the indictment claims that Mr. Mucic knew or had reason to know that his inferiors committed crimes? What is an inferior? Fourthly, the indictment goes on to say that it charges him for not taking measures that are expected of a person in a position of superiority. What does the term "is expected to do" mean? Can anyone be asked to answer for something that he -- because he didn't do something that is expected of him, can such a responsibility be defined as a war crime? The statute and relevant conventions say something quite different. Anyway, what can one expect of someone? One may demand or require something, somebody may have certain legal responsibilities and the like and these can be cited from the statute. But expectations are not a sufficient legal qualification for the acts that the client is being charged with. So, again, there is an error in the formulation of this position of superiority. This is not splitting hairs, but a point of substance. Fifth, the 7th point of the indictment, says that Mr. Zdravko Mucic was responsible for the work in the Celebici camp, but it doesn't say in what way. Sixth, the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Your Honours, was not an international conflict as is stated in the English text. The people is a populace and the nation is a national and there's nothing more to discuss. This is simply a matter of a misinterpretation. The allegation of the indictment that this was an international, interstate conflict simply does not correspond to the truth. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in tempore bos camelorum suspectorum (phoen) was an internationally recognised state inhabited by three constituent peoples. Uprisings in that state cannot be an international war, even if a rebellious party is assisted by another external state. These can be described as unrest and this may possibly be treated as a civil war. The aggression of the federal Republic of Yugoslavia is another matter. The alleged victims were not members of the armed forces of the federal Republic of Yugoslavia, so they cannot be protected persons according to the conventions of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, why don't you leave these arguments to your concluding address? Tell us something about the evidence that you want to lead. At this stage we're not going to give any finding on these issues. They are to be resolved at the end of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The evidence which you intend to lead the relations, how they are, how the evidence is connected to that. At this stage we're not going to decide whether it was international or internal conflict. We're not going to decide what really is implied by command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: All these things are interconnected because that is the content of the indictment in the way it has been worded and to which we have been objecting in the course of the proceedings. Of course, I will in my closing statement elaborate on all this in detail. These are just introductory remarks whereby I wish to prove the inconsistency of the indictment in relation to my client and that is precisely why I am going from point to point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At the end of your evidence when you're giving us your final concluding address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When you were to lead evidence, I asked you what you intended to say. And all I expected was what these witnesses you have told me, what they are saying when they come in today when the witness sits, not arguments which you intend to give or evidence which you as Counsel would be giving. Counsel is not expected to give evidence and many of the things you are saying now will not come into evidence by anyone, except from what you have said. I don't like interrupting Counsel, I expect them to use their judgement to present their arguments properly because you are being unfair. You have very little to say after you have led evidence. Now these are the same things you will say at the end of the Defence case. You have nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In law, many things could be said, but, of course, your ruling for me is final and, therefore, I will strictly abide by it. But I do not intend to speak at any length. I will also be referring to the witnesses that we intend to call, but simply to make the link between the witnesses of the Defence and the proceedings so far in the indictment itself, allow me to briefly tell you what it is that we intend to try to prove in the proceedings. That is, the areas we wish to cover, the arrest in Vienna and we will have witnesses about that. And it is important to note that in that connection that we will try to prove a series of omissions made by the Austrian police and the Austrian judiciary and that the evidence seized was seized in an illegal manner. As for the importance of Mr. Mucic's position and his command position and responsibility, here again my witnesses will prove that at the time it was not possible to organise forces which would be in any sense, regular. There were no military or police or political subordination. There was no law, no rules, no regulations regarding their implementation. Furthermore, we will prove that Mr. Mucic was not an officer, he was not appointed to any position of command. We will prove through our witnesses that he wore no insignia of such a position, nor had competencies stemming from such a position. We have already heard much to that effect from witnesses testimony so far, but our witnesses will also confirm that. They will tell us that for most of the time covered by the indictment, Mr. Mucic was absent from Konjic. So it is not possible for a real camp commander to be absent from his job in the middle of a war. Furthermore, as far as the actual international character of the conflict is concerned, we will prove that it was no international conflict. And as for inhumane conditions in Celebici and the illegal detention of civilians and alleged plunder of civilians and other detainees the Prosecution has not proven any of these allegations, but on the contrary, the witnesses of the Prosecution in their statements spoke in favour of Mr. Mucic so that I do not intend to call witnesses to those charges. I am referring also to the testimony of the expert witnesses and other witnesses heard in this Trial Chamber who were called by the first accused. So we will not duplicate the proceedings by trying to prove those points again. Finally allow me to conclude. In this short introduction, we wish to draw attention to what we consider to be crucial for establishing the truth. All these allegations and all the testimony and all the other evidence as required from me by Your Honours will be covered in my closing statement when I will also support those statements with references from these proceedings and other relevant sources. On this occasion, we have tried merely to highlight the main directions of the Defence emanating from the indictment and the whole case against my client, Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Some of my thesis will lend themselves to logical analysis. Everything else, I think, shows that there are no elements for any charges against my client, in spite of the case that we have before us. That would be all in brief in my introductory statement. And now, with your permission, Your Honours, we should like to present our case and our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may it please the court. May I address you before my learned colleague calls his first witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there may be a problem in my understanding of your comments, but what I heard at the beginning of your remarks addressed to my colleague is that the Defence of Mr. Delalic has lost some right. So I would like to ask this to be corrected and clarified before we continue, because I should like to refer to Rule 84, according to which before the Prosecutor presents his Defence, each party may make an introductory address. The Defence of Mr. Delalic did not make such an opening statement. The Defence of Mr. Mucic did make an opening statement, but with the permission of this Trial Chamber, it was allowed to do so subsequently. The second sentence of this same Rule is clear. The Defence may, however, elect to make its statement after the conclusion of the Prosecutor's presentation of evidence and before the presentation of evidence for the Defence. Mr. Delalic's Defence opted for a brief opening statement indicating what evidence it intends to call and did not feel it necessary to make any lengthy opening address. For this reason I don't understand. Maybe it is misinterpretation. I do not understand your remark that we have lost our right to an opening statement. We made that statement before the presentation of the Defence, saying that we would be calling expert witnesses and other witnesses who would deny the allegations in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You had full opportunity to make any addresses you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you read the rules carefully, it says you either opt to make it at the opening or after the presentation of the case of the Prosecution. It is a very clear -- Rule 85 is very clear. You have not concluded, you still have a right to make your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to make it clear. We will not have any more opening statements, but at the end we will avail ourselves of the right from Rule 86 to make our closing statement, closing arguments. I just wanted to make sure that we hadn't lost any right, as I had gathered from the interpretation. So that at the end of the presentation of the evidence we will present our closing arguments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, you can now call your witness, Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is your witness is a protected witness, the witness you are going to call? Because the curtains have to go down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, you inform the technical crew about the distortion of the faces so that they couldn't be recognised from outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please take your seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: To make sure of the identity of the witness, we will show the witness a document with her name and date of birth, and the witness simply has to agree whether that is indeed her name and her date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, and since we are going to have some introductory questions to begin with, questions which concern the identity, so the witness might be recognised by anyone, I would kindly ask you to move into closed session, just for this part of this introductory part of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will rather be a private session, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of June, at 10.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: Pages 13185 to 13284 redacted - in private session
